ety.text: Pre-Greekbor. Ancient Greek βόμβος (bómbos)bor. Latin bombusder. Italian bombabor. French bombebor. English bomb From French bombe, from Italian bomba, from Latin bombus (“a booming sound”), from Ancient Greek βόμβος (bómbos, “booming, humming, buzzing”), imitative of the sound itself. Doublet of bombe. Compare boom.

senses.d: An explosive device used or intended as a weapon, especially, one dropped from an aircraft.
ex: The size of the ground hole crater from the blast indicates it was a bomb.

senses.d: The atomic bomb.
ex: During the Cold War, everyone worried about the bomb sometimes.

senses.d: Events or conditions that have a speedy destructive effect.
ex: "The hard Brexiteers have built a bomb under the UK automotive industry and the EU have lit it," they said.

senses.d: A grenade, mortar shell, or artillery shell.
ex: And the rockets' red glare, the bombs bursting in air / Gave proof through the night that our flag was still there

senses.d: Any explosive charge.
ex: The mineworkers are setting their bombs.

senses.d: A bag or balloon containing a substance such as water, flour, or paint, designed to burst and splatter.
ex: The children are playing with water bombs in the garden.
Activists threw paint bombs at the famous artwork.

senses.d: Anything that is at risk of exploding (literally) or that has exploded.
ex: That turkey fryer is a bomb waiting to go off.
The gas leak tragically turned the house into a bomb.

senses.d: A fart.
ex: He just dropped a bomb.

senses.d: A failure; an unpopular commercial product.
ex: box-office bomb
The movie was a bomb and so was my next film, Balboa, in which I played a scheming real estate tycoon.

senses.d: A car in poor condition.
ex: Nowadays, an old bomb simply won’t pass the inspection.
We′ve got the money and it just feels ridiculous to let you drive around in that old bomb.

senses.d: To attack using one or more bombs; to bombard.
ex: Essendon was bombed in the early hours of 3 September 1916; a few houses and part of the church were destroyed, and two sisters killed.

senses.d: To attack or annoy in the manner of a bombing.
To jump into water in a squatting position, with the arms wrapped around the legs, in order to maximise the resulting splash.
To add an excessive amount of chlorine to a pool when it has not been maintained properly.
To move at high speed.
ex: I was bombing down the road on my motorbike.

senses.d: To make oneself drunk.
ex: The calendar was selling Moctezuma beer, so I had one of them in her honor while Murray bombed himself with the mezcal.

senses.d: To cover an area in many graffiti tags.
ex: It is often used to collect other writer's tags, and future plans for bombing and piecing.

senses.d: To fail dismally.
ex: I totally bombed that exam.
She was the reason why he bombed the interview. He just couldn′t seem to get her out of his mind.

senses.d: To crash.
To make a smelly mess in (a toilet).
Great, awesome.
ex: Have you tried the new tacos from that restaurant? They're pretty bomb!
